job.style: a comparison of two related ideas

passage: In India, secularism is defined by the principle of 'principled distance,' which allows the state to intervene in religious affairs to protect individual rights. Unlike some Western models that demand a total separation where the state ignores religion entirely, Indian secularism permits the government to support religious institutions if they serve the public good. For instance, the state may provide financial aid to minority-run schools to ensure equitable access to education for all children. Furthermore, the government has the authority to step in and ban harmful practices, such as untouchability, even if they are rooted in religious tradition. This ensures that no single group dominates others and that every citizen can practice their faith without fear. Secularism does not mean the state must ban all religious symbols or prayers in public spaces; rather, it means the state remains neutral and treats all religions with equal respect. By balancing intervention and non-interference, the Indian state protects the fundamental rights of its citizens while preventing religious domination. This approach acknowledges that religion is a significant part of social life, but it must not be used to violate the dignity or freedom of any individual.

items.evidence: In India, secularism is defined by the principle of 'principled distance,' which allows the state to intervene in religious affairs to protect individual rights.
items.q: What does 'principled distance' allow the Indian state to do?
options: Step into religious matters to protect people's rights
Stay equally far from every religion at all times
Help whichever religion it likes the most
Leave religion alone, even when it harms people
items.explain: Principled distance lets the state intervene in religious affairs to protect each person's rights.

wrong.why: thinks principled distance means never getting involved
thinks the state picks a favourite religion
thinks the state must never interfere in religion

items.evidence: For instance, the state may provide financial aid to minority-run schools to ensure equitable access to education for all children.
items.q: The state gives money to a minority-run school. What does this show about Indian secularism?
options: It may support religious groups for the public good
It has stopped being secular by funding religion
It favours whichever religion it likes best
It follows the Western model of total separation
items.explain: Indian secularism allows aid to minority schools so all children get fair access to education.

wrong.why: thinks funding a religious school ends secularism
thinks aid means the state has a favourite
mixes up the Indian and Western models

items.evidence: Furthermore, the government has the authority to step in and ban harmful practices, such as untouchability, even if they are rooted in religious tradition.
items.q: Untouchability was part of an old religious tradition. Why could the government still ban it?
options: Because it hurt people's rights and dignity
Because the state is against all religion
Because one religion was dominating another religion
Because it was never part of any religion
items.explain: The state can ban harmful practices like untouchability, even when they are rooted in religious tradition.

wrong.why: thinks a secular state opposes religion
thinks domination happens only between religions
misses that the passage says it was rooted in tradition

items.evidence: Secularism does not mean the state must ban all religious symbols or prayers in public spaces; rather, it means the state remains neutral and treats all religions with equal respect.
items.q: A city has temples, mosques and churches along its main roads. What would a secular Indian state do?
options: Treat all of them with the same respect
Remove all of them from public spaces
Keep only the religion most people follow
Discourage all of them, as it opposes religion
items.explain: Secularism does not ban religious symbols; the state stays neutral and respects all religions equally.

wrong.why: thinks secularism bans religion in public spaces
thinks a secular country has one religion
thinks a secular state is against religion
